name: Ultrasound scan: what happens and is it safe
summary: An ultrasound scan uses sound waves, not radiation, to make live pictures. This guide covers the gel, the full bladder, internal scans and results.
keyPoints: An ultrasound scan uses sound waves rather than radiation, and the NHS describes the sound waves used as safe.
A water-based gel goes on the skin, and a small probe is moved over the area being scanned.
Pelvic and bladder scans usually need a full bladder, and the hospital or clinic explains how to prepare.
Some people have an internal (transvaginal) scan.

body.heading: What is an ultrasound scan?
body.body: An ultrasound scan uses high-frequency sound waves to make a picture of the inside of the body. The sound waves bounce off different parts of the body, and the echoes are picked up by a probe and turned into a moving image. It does not use radiation or X-rays. NHS and NHS trust pages describe ultrasound being used to look inside the body, to guide procedures such as biopsy and drainage, and during pregnancy. It can also help to guide a biopsy or the draining of fluid.

body.heading: What happens during the scan?
body.body: Gel is put on the skin over the area and a small probe is moved across it. The gel is water-based and washes off easily, and trust leaflets say it will not stain clothing. The NHS says an ultrasound scan takes around 10 to 45 minutes, and may take longer. Afterwards the gel can be wiped off and the person can get dressed.

body.heading: Why do some scans need a full bladder?
body.body: For pelvic and bladder scans, people are usually asked to arrive with a full bladder. Trust leaflets explain that a full bladder gives a clearer picture because sound waves travel more easily through fluid. Leaflets ask people not to empty their bladder until after the scan, and say a toilet is nearby afterwards. Scans of some organs, such as the liver, may need no food for several hours beforehand. The hospital or clinic tells people how to prepare for their type of scan.

body.heading: What are the different kinds of ultrasound scan?
body.body: The usual scan is external, with the probe on the skin. Some people have a transvaginal (internal) scan. For this scan the probe is disinfected, covered with a protective sheath and lubricated with gel. People usually need to empty their bladder first for an internal scan. Ultrasound can also be used to look at blood flow and at whether blood vessels are narrowed or blocked.

body.heading: Is an ultrasound scan safe?
body.body: The NHS says the sound waves used in ultrasound scans are safe, and that ultrasound scans do not use radiation. An NHS maternity leaflet says scans are painless and have no known side effects. One hospital notes that standard ultrasound gel is not sterile, so there is a very small risk of infection in some circumstances. People with a latex allergy are asked to tell the department beforehand so latex-free products can be used.

body.heading: When are the results shared?
body.body: The images are reviewed by the specialist who carried out the scan. The report goes to the doctor or team who requested the scan. The NHS says results may be given at the end of the appointment, or can take a few weeks, depending on the reason for the scan.
